<!-- BEAT 2 — Contesto: who draws the line, and how -->

## *Who draws the line — and how?*

![](../img/storyboard/sb-03_02.png){fig-align="center" width="76%"}

::: {.notes}
Nel cap. 02 il confine lo tracciava la mano di Elena. Ora lo traccia *l'algoritmo*. Tre famiglie principali, tre idee diverse di cosa sia una "linea sensata".
:::

## Three families of algorithms

- **$k$-NN** — the *training data themselves* define the boundary (lazy).
- **Linear / SVM** — one *global cut* with the widest margin (and *bend the space first* if needed: the **kernel trick**).
- **Ensembles / Random Forest** — many weak voters; the **majority vote** beats any single one (as long as each is better than chance).

Each family carries its own *prior* on what a sensible boundary looks like.

::: {.notes}
Cifra del capitolo (da landare a voce): a parità di dati, la *forma di confine* che ogni famiglia sa produrre è diversa — e quella forma, più del campione, decide cosa si vede.
:::

<!-- BEAT 3 — Sfida / kNN -->

## *$k$-NN: the data themselves decide.*

![](../img/storyboard/sb-03_03.png){fig-align="center" width="78%"}

::: {.notes}
A voce: $k$NN non fa regole, **memorizza** il training; copia la maggioranza dei $k$ vicini. Il confine *si incolla ai dati*.
:::

## $k$-Nearest Neighbor — the recipe

For a new point $x$:

1. Find its $k$ nearest training points (by some distance metric).
2. Take a **majority vote** among their class labels.
3. Assign that class to $x$.

**Rule of thumb in this chapter:** $k = 3$.

The decision regions are *defined by the training points themselves* — **piecewise** boundaries that hug each cluster's edge.

::: {.notes}
- A voce: niente parametri appresi, il training set *è* il modello (lazy learner).
- $k$ è un *iperparametro*: $k$ piccolo → confine sinuoso (overfit, gancio cap. 04); $k$ grande → smussato.
:::

<!-- BEAT 4 — Nodo: kernel trick -->

## *One straight cut. The shape is in the folds.*

![](../img/one-cut-star.jpg){fig-align="center" width="72%"}

::: {.notes}
Analogia fisica del kernel trick. Lasciate la slide qualche secondo (riconoscono la stella di carta).

- Teorema fold-and-cut (Demaine–Demaine–Lubiw, 1998): ogni poligono da un foglio con **un solo taglio dritto**, se piegato bene.
- Punch line: *il taglio è uno; è la piega che decide la forma.* = classificatore fermo, cambia la rappresentazione.
:::

## *Bend the space, not the algorithm.*

![](../img/storyboard/sb-03_04.png){fig-align="center" width="84%"}

::: {.notes}
A voce: dati non separabili → SVM non cambia algoritmo, cambia *coordinate* (la $\phi$). La linea torna a funzionare in alto, la riproietti come curva. Kernel trick = re-coordinatizzazione.
:::

## Linear SVM and the kernel trick

**Linear SVM**: find the **widest-margin hyperplane** between classes:
$$f(x) = \text{sgn}(w^\top x + b).$$

When classes are **not** linearly separable, apply a feature map $\phi:\mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^D$ first:
$$\phi(y_1, y_2) \;=\; \bigl(y_1^2,\; y_2^2,\; \sqrt{2}\,y_1 y_2\bigr).$$

Then cut with a hyperplane *in the $\phi$-space*; project back as a **smooth curve** in the original space.

The classifier did *not* change — *what it sees* did.

::: {.notes}
Take-away: kernel trick = cambio di rappresentazione, non nuovo algoritmo.

Aggancia all'item 02: cerchi concentrici → $(y_1, y_2) \mapsto (y_1^2, y_2^2)$ → separabili.
:::

<!-- BEAT 5 — Metodo: ensembles + 3-column board (perno del sommativo) -->

## *Many weak voters beat one strong.*

![](../img/storyboard/sb-03_05.png){fig-align="center" width="84%"}

::: {.notes}
A voce: tanti alberelli ($p$ appena $> 0.5$) votano; il voto migliora con $m$ solo se $p > 0.5$.

Flag: il **3-column board** (kNN · SVM · RF) è il perno del sommativo.
:::

## Random Forest and the majority vote

**Random Forest** = many small decision trees, each trained on a *bootstrapped* slice of the data, combined by **majority vote**.

For $m$ independent weak classifiers each with per-classifier accuracy $p$:

- if $p > 0.5$ → vote accuracy goes **up toward $1$** as $m$ grows;
- if $p < 0.5$ → vote accuracy goes **down toward $0$** as $m$ grows.

Voting *amplifies whichever direction $p$ points*. Hence the **$p > 0.5$ requirement**.

::: {.notes}
Punto quantitativo: voto di maggioranza ≠ media — è una *binomial tail* che si concentra al crescere di $m$. L'item 03 testa la direzione.
:::

## Three families, three boundary shapes

| Family | Shape of the boundary it produces |
|---|---|
| **$k$-NN** | piecewise wiggly curve hugging the training points |
| **Linear SVM** | one straight cut |
| **Kernel SVM** | smooth curved boundary (a hyperplane in $\phi$-space, projected back) |
| **Random Forest** | axis-aligned staircase of small rectangles (voted) |

Same data, different priors → different region shapes.

::: {.notes}
Checklist visiva del sommativo: ogni colonna del board ricade in una di queste shape.

Cautela: il termine tecnico è *inductive bias* — NON promuoverlo in vocabolario studente.
:::

## *Perfect on training. On a new patient?*

![](../img/storyboard/sb-03_06.png){fig-align="center" width="78%"}

::: {.notes}
A voce — *paradosso dell'iperaderenza*: chi si attacca meglio ai dati visti generalizza peggio. $k=1$ = errore zero sul training, sbaglia il primo nuovo paziente. Cliff-hanger al cap. 04.
:::

## Pre-hook → chapter 4: model selection

Three reasonable boundaries on the same twelve patients.

Among them, $k$-NN with $k=1$ *never* misclassifies a single training patient — its risk on the sample is exactly $0$. **And that very perfection is what dooms it on new patients.**

How do we tell *good fits* from *fakes*? That is **model selection** — next.

::: {.notes}
Pre-hook scriptato al cap. 04. La parola *"fake"* è voluta: il cap. 04 la sviluppa con train/validation/test e CV. Lasciate aperto il paradosso.
:::

<!-- Item 01 — MCQ — boundary to family -->

## Item 01 — Question

A classifier produces a decision boundary that can be described as: a **wiggly, piecewise curve that hugs the training data closely**, with small detours around individual points. The regions look as if *carved by the training points themselves*.

Which algorithm family most likely produced this boundary?

- **A)** $k$-Nearest Neighbor (with small $k$).
- **B)** Support-Vector Machine, **linear** (non-kernel).
- **C)** Random Forest.
- **D)** Support-Vector Machine with a **non-linear kernel**.

::: {.notes}
Item 01 — Comprehension / MCQ / low-medium. Obj. 1 (read family off boundary shape). Vedi `course/03-algorithm-examples/items/item_01_boundary-to-family_mcq.md`.
:::

## Item 01 — Solution (write yours)

::: {.notes}
Lascio 60 secondi. Se la classe esita tra A e D, è il momento di richiamare la tabella shape: $k$NN = *piecewise wiggly*; kernel SVM = *smooth curve*.
:::

## Item 01 — Solution

**Correct: A — $k$-Nearest Neighbor (small $k$).**

The defining clue is *the boundary follows the data*. $k$NN labels by the majority class of the $k$ nearest training neighbours, so the regions are defined *by the training points themselves* — a piecewise, data-hugging boundary.

Why the distractors are wrong:

- **B** (linear SVM): a single *straight* line — the opposite of wiggly.
- **C** (RF): an **axis-aligned staircase** of small rectangles — blocky, not smoothly wiggly.
- **D** (kernel SVM): a **smooth curve**, not piecewise.

::: {.notes}
Riprendere la tabella shape del beat 5 mentre la classe guarda la soluzione.
:::

<!-- Item 02 — Applicativa — Kernel trick -->

## Item 02 — Question {.smaller}

Eight patients in 2D: red on the **unit circle** $y_1^2 + y_2^2 = 1$ (A,B,C,D), blue on the circle $y_1^2 + y_2^2 = 9$ (E,F,G,H) — *concentric*.

A non-linear feature map is given:
$$\phi(y_1, y_2) \;=\; (y_1^2,\; y_2^2) \;=\; (X_1, X_2).$$

1. **Argue** why **no straight line** in $(y_1, y_2)$ separates red from blue (1–2 sentences).
2. **Tabulate** $(X_1, X_2) = \phi(y_1, y_2)$ for the 8 patients.
3. **State a linear rule** in $(X_1, X_2)$ — of the form *"red if $aX_1 + bX_2 < c$"* with specific $a, b, c$ — that separates the two classes perfectly. Verify on one red, one blue.
4. The classifier did *not* change. **What changed**, and why is that enough?

::: {.notes}
Item 02 — Application / applicativa / medium. Obj. 2 (kernel trick come re-coordinatizzazione). Tempo atteso: ~5′ (con i calcoli). Rubrica: `course/03-algorithm-examples/rubriche/rubrica_02_apply-the-kernel-trick.md`.
:::

## Item 02 — Solution (write yours)

::: {.notes}
Soluzione a portata di mano mentre scrivono: red → $\{(1,0),(0,1)\}$, blue → $\{(9,0),(0,9)\}$. Somma $X_1+X_2$: $1$ red, $9$ blue → taglio $X_1+X_2 < 5$.
:::

## Item 02 — Solution {.smaller}

**1.** Red and blue are *concentric*: every direction from origin contains both a red (distance 1) and a blue (distance 3) patient. Any straight line has *both* classes on the same side.

**2.** $\phi(y_1, y_2) = (y_1^2, y_2^2)$: all reds map to $\{(1,0), (0,1)\}$; all blues map to $\{(9,0), (0,9)\}$. Note **all reds satisfy $X_1 + X_2 = 1$**, all blues $X_1 + X_2 = 9$.

**3.** Linear rule: *"red if $X_1 + X_2 < 5$, blue otherwise"* (any $c \in (1, 9)$ works). Verify: A $\to (1, 0) \to 1 < 5$ ✓ red; E $\to (9, 0) \to 9 \ge 5$ ✓ blue.

**4.** The **data changed** — same 8 patients re-coordinatised by $\phi$ — exposing distance-from-origin info hidden in $(y_1, y_2)$. The classifier is still a straight cut. The boundary $X_1 + X_2 = 5$ in $\phi$-space ↔ **circle** $y_1^2 + y_2^2 = 5$ in the original space — the boundary the data actually wanted.

::: {.notes}
Il punto pedagogico: cambiando il *dato* (le coordinate), un classificatore lineare risolve un problema non-linearmente-separabile. *Il classificatore non è cambiato.* Questa è la frase chiave da far ripetere alla classe.
:::

<!-- Item 03 — MCQ — Majority vote direction -->

## Item 03 — Question

Two ensembles, each $100$ weak classifiers combined by majority vote (assume independence).

- **Configuration X**: per-classifier accuracy $p = 0.55$.
- **Configuration Y**: per-classifier accuracy $p = 0.45$.

Which statement about the majority-vote accuracy is correct?

- **A)** X's vote is **more accurate than $0.55$**, and Y's vote is **less accurate than $0.45$**.
- **B)** Both votes are more accurate than their single classifiers — more is always better.
- **C)** X's vote $\approx p = 0.55$ — averaging gives the average.
- **D)** Y's vote is more accurate than X's, because $p = 0.45$ leaves more room for correction.

::: {.notes}
Item 03 — Application / MCQ / medium. Obj. 3 (direction of binomial-vote concentration; $p>0.5$ requirement). Vedi `course/03-algorithm-examples/items/item_03_majority-vote-direction_mcq.md`.
:::

## Item 03 — Solution (write yours)

::: {.notes}
Punto chiave: il voto di maggioranza non *media*, **concentra**. La direzione di concentramento dipende dal segno di $p - 0.5$. Se la classe esita tra A e B, fermarsi sul *perché* B è sbagliato — è il fraintendimento più comune.
:::

## Item 03 — Solution

**Correct: A.** The majority-vote accuracy **concentrates** as $m$ grows:

- if $p > 0.5$ → vote accuracy goes **up toward $1$**;
- if $p < 0.5$ → vote accuracy goes **down toward $0$**.

So X ($p = 0.55$) → vote $\gg 0.55$, close to $1$. Y ($p = 0.45$) → vote $\ll 0.45$, close to $0$.

Why the distractors are wrong:

- **B** misses the $p > 0.5$ requirement. Y's vote actually *worsens*.
- **C** confuses majority vote with arithmetic average. The vote returns the *most-voted label*, not the probability $p$.
- **D** is the "underdog correction" intuition — wrong by symmetry: voting amplifies whatever signal is there.

::: {.notes}
Take-away: $p > 0.5$ NON è cosmetica, è la condizione necessaria perché un ensemble funzioni. Si concentra su quello che c'è — bene se $p > 0.5$, male se no.
:::

<!-- Item 04 — Argomentativa — Which algorithm fits these data -->

## Item 04 — Question

A 2D scatter shows two classes forming **interlocked half-moons** (clearly non-linearly separable: every straight line crosses both classes).

> *"Which algorithm should I use on these data, and why?"*

Using **only this chapter's language** — *shape of decision regions each family produces* — argue in two parts:

1. **Propose one algorithm family that would FIT.** Name its boundary shape and argue why that shape *matches* the data.
2. **Identify one algorithm family that would NOT fit.** Name its shape and argue why it *cannot match*. Use the **0/1 risk on the sample** (ch. 02) to name the concrete consequence.

::: {.notes}
Item 04 — Argumentation / argomentativa / medium. Obj. 1 + light Obj. 2. Rubrica: `course/03-algorithm-examples/rubriche/rubrica_04_simpler-is-safer-critique.md`.
:::

## Item 04 — Solution (write yours)

::: {.notes}
Slide bianca: il punto non è "qual è la risposta giusta" (parte 1 ammette ≥ 1 risposta valida) ma *legarla alla shape del confine*. Penalizzare solo la *generica* risposta "kNN è meglio" senza nominare la shape.
:::

## Item 04 — Solution

**Part 1 — Any one of these fits**, provided the shape is named:

- **Kernel SVM** → *smooth curve* (hyperplane in $\phi$-space, projected back); can enclose a half-moon.
- **$k$-NN** → *piecewise wiggly curve* defined by the training points; naturally follows half-moon clusters.
- **Random Forest** → *axis-aligned staircase* voted by many trees; carves half-moons into correctly-coloured rectangles (binomial vote concentrates as long as each tree has $p > 0.5$).

**Part 2 — Linear (non-kernel) SVM does NOT fit.** Boundary: a **single straight cut**. On interlocked half-moons, *no straight line* can put each class on one side. Concrete consequence: **high 0/1 risk on the sample** — many patients on the wrong side, average 0/1 loss is large. The mismatch is structural.

::: {.notes}
Reveal: il punto chiave è "the shape of decision regions each family can produce". Premiare le risposte che *nominano* la shape, non quelle che semplicemente menzionano l'algoritmo.
:::

## Summative — *Three algorithms, one dataset* {.inverse .smaller background-color="#1F4257"}

Three groups, **one** scatter (non-linearly separable). Each group is assigned one algorithm card and a one-sentence question:

- **Group A — $k$-NN ($k = 3$).** Sketch the boundary. Q: *"What happens to the boundary if $k$ is doubled?"*
- **Group B — SVM** (pick *linear* or *kernel*). Sketch. Q: *"This data is not linearly separable — do you pick linear or kernel, and which feature map?"*
- **Group C — Random Forest (~50 trees).** Sketch. Q: *"5 trees, each $p = 0.6$, majority vote — more or less accurate than 1 tree with $p = 0.6$? Why?"*

All sketches go on a **3-column board** ($k$NN · SVM · RF), in-person + remote side by side.

::: {.notes}
Sommativo — ultimi ~10′ (min 24-34). Timing:

- ~2′ assegnare · ~5′ sketch + 1-liner · ~30″ silent beat (ognuno scrive sull'objective non toccato) · ~2′30″ reveal.
- Poll Slido sulla shape (5 opzioni, non 3): piecewise · smooth curve · staircase · straight line · concentric circles.
- Duale: lavagna 3 colonne (foto + drawing tool remoti) = unico artefatto.
- **Non dichiarare vincitori**: "il migliore su pazienti NUOVI?" resta aperta → gancio cap. 04.
:::

## Summative — Solution (write yours)

::: {.notes}
Reveal: nomino le 3 colonne — piecewise · max-margin/smooth curve · vote-of-cuts — leggendo la shape dal board. Poi 3 one-liner cross-objective a caso dai silent-beat (verifica obj. 2 e 3 oltre il gruppo).
:::

## Summative — Solution {.smaller}

| Family | Shape on the board | One-liner answer |
|---|---|---|
| **$k$-NN ($k{=}3$)** | piecewise, hugging individual points | larger $k$ → **smoother** (averages more neighbours) |
| **SVM** | *if linear*: straight line + must say why it fails ; *if kernel*: smooth curve + name $\phi$ | pick **kernel** (e.g. $\phi(y_1, y_2) = (y_1^2, y_2^2, \sqrt{2}\,y_1 y_2)$) |
| **RF (~50 trees)** | axis-aligned staircase | **more accurate** — majority vote concentrates on correct answer when $p > 0.5$ |

**Live signal of mastery:** the class can point at the board and say — *unprompted* — *"same data, different algorithms, different region shapes → different carvings"*.

*Take-home challenge:* among these three, which one will hold on **patients never seen**? — Chapter 4.

::: {.notes}
Chiudi col cliff-hanger cap. 04. Se un gruppo dice "il nostro è il più accurato" → rispondi "su questi 12 sì — ma su un paziente mai visto?" Non chiudere: è il gancio.
:::
